candidates.name: Dar Ben Abdallah Museum
candidates.content: A small but interesting folk museum within an 18th-century palace in the medina, covering the everyday life of a rich merchant in the Ottoman era with exhibits including faience, stucco ornament, costumes and furniture.

candidates.name: Bardo Museum
candidates.hours: Tue - Sun. Sep 16th - May 30th: 09:30-16:30. Jun 1st - Sep 15th: 09:00-17:00
candidates.content: Occupying the 13th-century palace of the Ottoman-era bey (ruler) and renowned for its extensive collection of Roman mosaics, although the (huge) collection covers Tunisia's entire existence from the prehistoric era until the Ottom

candidates.name: Uthina
candidates.hours: 09:00 - 17:00, it closes 2 hr later in summer
candidates.content: It was an ancient Roman-Berber city. Now it features remains of a fortress, cisterns, an aqueduct, a triumphal arch, a theatre, an amphitheater, a basilica with a circular crypt, and a bridge. Many mosaics are to be found there as

candidates.name: Tunis Medina
candidates.content: The world heritage listed old town is a must-see colorful, crowded labyrinth of decorated old houses, vaults and street vendors. You can move around by foot only. You get a feel of medieval life.

candidates.name: Cathedral of St. Vincent de Paul
candidates.content: Built in 1882, this is the largest surviving building from Tunis' colonial era, in the neo-Romanesque style. It was named after St. Vincent de Paul, a priest in the region who was sold as a slave and fought slavery after he was li

candidates.name: Grande Mosquée Zitouna
candidates.content: The largest and oldest mosque in Tunisia and an important landmark, this Aghlabite mosque dates back to the 8th century, although the distinctive square minaret is a much later 19th century addition. It has 160 pillars, that come

candidates.name: Sidi Youssef Dey Mosque
candidates.content: Opened in 1631, this was the first Ottoman mosque to be built in Tunis. It is the largest Hanafi mosque in the city, was extensively restored in the late 19th century and is now a part of the University of Ez-Zitouna. A historical

candidates.name: Medersa Bachia
candidates.content: Quran school from the 18th century, a monument since 1912. It is notable for its public fountain located outside the entrance. In the 1980s it was converted into an artisan school with students studying leather craft, jewellery an

candidates.name: Bab El Bahr
candidates.content: The gate to the sea, which remains unchanged since its erection in 1848. It can be found on the Avenue de France. Before it was built it was an empty space where you could see the Mediterranean on one side and Lake Tunis on the ot

candidates.name: Tourbet el-Bey
candidates.content: An impressive 18th-century mausoleum, the final resting place for over 160 princes and ministers and their families. The eight-pointed star inside represents the doors to paradise.

candidates.name: Place de la Victoire
candidates.content: A lively square at the entrance to the medina. Bordered with shops, cafés and the ornamented building which houses the High Commission of the United Kingdom.

candidates.name: Bab Saadoun
candidates.content: Another gate, constructed in 1350 with one arch, then rebuilt in 1881 with three arches to facilitate commerce.

candidates.name: Avenue de France
candidates.content: One of the busiest streets of Tunis. It is bordered with shops and eateries and several architecturally interesting buildings.

candidates.name: Parc du Belvédère
candidates.content: A large park created during the French rule and featuring palm trees, mimosas and azaleas and a great view of Tunis and the lake. Sadly, the park has seen better days and graffiti is commonplace. Still, it's a popular place for lo

candidates.name: Hôtel de Ville
candidates.content: Not a hotel, but the city hall. The building was inaugurated in 1998 and is a combination of traditional and modern architecture with large windows, Middle Eastern patterns and arches. The city hall also features a lot of Tunisian

candidates.name: Chambre des Conseillers
candidates.content: Finished in 2005, this building used to house the upper house of the Parliament of Tunisia. It didn't serve this purpose for very long; after the 2011 revolution the Tunisian parliament was made unicameral and the counselor chambe

candidates.name: Théâtre Municipal
candidates.content: A pretty white Art-Deco building, worth seeing in its own right even if you're not going there to see a play or concert (also see the Do section).

candidates.name: Tunis Clock Tower
candidates.content: The iconic clock tower is one of the city's most visible landmarks.

candidates.name: Al-Fateh Mosque
candidates.content: A large white mosque north of downtown.

candidates.name: Bar Jamaica
candidates.content: On the 10th floor of the Hotel el-Hana International, this is a funky and popular destination for locals and foreigners, with music and outdoor seating available.

candidates.name: Le Boeuf sur le Toit
candidates.content: The name means "the Ox on the Roof", and trendy people come for food, drinks, live music, DJs, and a dance floor.

candidates.name: Hotel Africa Lobby Bar
candidates.content: A bit smoky, but has all of the local drinks save Stella, and is one of the few places that serves alcohol during Ramadan.

candidates.name: Piano Bar
candidates.content: A good place for a drink, located in a 5-star hotel.

candidates.name: Panorama Medina
candidates.price: DT2 for tea, DT5 for shisha
candidates.content: Beautifully decorated café and tea house in the heart of the Medina. A large rooftop offers stunning views over the old buildings and of the many mosques around.

candidates.name: Brasserie les 2 Avenues
candidates.content: Great location with views over Avenue Habib Bourguiba.

candidates.name: Café M'Rabet
candidates.content: Cafe and restaurant.

candidates.name: Café de Paris
candidates.content: One of the major cafes along the avenue, very popular and lively.

candidates.name: The Corner
candidates.content: Breakfast cafe.

candidates.name: Restaurant Ojja Chouchou
candidates.content: Popular so it may be busy, but the service is fast so people will be coming and going. Large portions.

candidates.name: Etoile de La Medina
candidates.content: Tucked away it is something special. Traditional food and decor. Welcoming with plentiful amounts of food.

candidates.name: La Sirène
candidates.content: You pick the fish from their market and they fry it right there. Indoor and outdoor seating. Can be busy so enjoy the water views while you wait.

candidates.name: L'Orient
candidates.content: The steaks are bland, the fish good and local food such as Berber Lamb is excellent. The service is prompt.

candidates.name: Dar el-Jeld
candidates.content: Reservations online. Perhaps the best of the restaurants in Tunis, this restaurant pays attention to every single detail. The food is excellent, and the management speaks English and French fluently, and can recommend various dish

candidates.name: Café de Paris Brasserie
candidates.content: A good restaurant with a beautiful interior and some outdoor tables. You can choose among pizza, couscous and a variety of salad. Also serves alcohol.

candidates.name: La Mamma
candidates.content: Very cosy restaurant on several floors. Good Italian inspired food. Has live music and is open to midnight.

candidates.name: Restaurant Dar Slah
candidates.content: Luxurious seafood restaurant with a large terrace surrounded by palm trees. In medina so can be hard to find, look for the yellow sign and door.

candidates.name: Halfaouine
candidates.content: A cheap, traditional food market, located at Place Halfaouine, near the railway station.
